cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 6 · Level 3 — Maternal and Newborn Nursing

bullets.label: Student Learning Notes · Level 3 — Global Nursing Professional

cards.title: Welcome to Level 3
cards.body: The highest level of the GNPS learning pathway. Global Nursing Professionals improve maternal and newborn outcomes beyond the individual bedside — leading safety initiatives, strengthening referral systems, mentoring staff, using data and championing equitable, respectful maternity care.

bullets.label: Advanced capability in perinatal governance and safety
Contributing to worldwide maternal and neonatal health

cards.title: What You Will Learn
cards.body: Throughout Level 3, you will strengthen your ability to:

bullets.label: Lead respectful and safe maternity services
Strengthen systems for recognising maternal and neonatal deterioration
Analyse outcomes, near misses and quality indicators
Support equitable access and culturally safe care
Mentor teams in clinical judgement and emergency response
Contribute to global maternal and newborn health improvement

cards.title: Why This Learning Matters
cards.body: Preventable maternal and newborn harm often reflects system weaknesses rather than individual failure:

bullets.label: Global Nursing Professionals recognise these connections and lead practical improvements.

cards.title: YOUR LEARNING GOAL
cards.body: Lead. Improve. Contribute.

bullets.label: By completing Level 3, you will be prepared to
bullets.text: By completing Level 3, you will be prepared to lead maternity and newborn quality initiatives, use evidence and data to improve systems, support colleagues, and contribute to healthier beginnings — locally and globally.

cards.title: SECTION 1
cards.body: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services

bullets.label: Leadership in maternal and newborn care means
bullets.text: Leadership in maternal and newborn care means creating services where women and families are treated with dignity, staff can raise concerns, and evidence-based care is available reliably. Global Nursing Professionals model respectful practice and strengthen clinical governance.

cards.title: Section 1 — Core Concepts
cards.body: Respectful Maternity Care

bullets.label: Women deserve privacy, dignity, informed choice
bullets.text: Women deserve privacy, dignity, informed choice and freedom from discrimination. Respectful care is both an ethical responsibility and a patient safety issue.

bullets.label: Staff must feel confident to question abnormal
bullets.text: Staff must feel confident to question abnormal findings, request help and report near misses without fear. This culture enables earlier intervention.

bullets.label: Regular drills and team simulation strengthen
bullets.text: Regular drills and team simulation strengthen responses to haemorrhage, eclampsia, shoulder dystocia and neonatal resuscitation.

bullets.label: Policies, audit, credentialing, incident review
bullets.text: Policies, audit, credentialing, incident review and outcome monitoring provide oversight and support consistent, accountable practice.

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: A maternity unit identifies that junior staff hesitate to activate the emergency team.

bullets.label: Result: Emergency activation becomes earlier and staff confidence measurably improves.
Make respectful care a measurable standard
Create a culture where concerns are heard
Use simulation to build team readiness
Link policy with visible leadership and accountability
Supportive debriefing sessions follow each drill

cards.title: SECTION 2
cards.body: Improving Maternal and Neonatal Safety Systems

bullets.label: Preventable harm often involves delayed
bullets.text: Preventable harm often involves delayed recognition, communication failure or weak referral pathways. Systems thinking helps leaders understand how work conditions influence outcomes — and how to redesign them effectively.

cards.title: Section 2 — Core Concepts
cards.body: Deterioration Systems

bullets.label: Maternal early warning tools and neonatal
bullets.text: Maternal early warning tools and neonatal observation pathways support recognition — but must be completed accurately and linked to a timely clinical response.

bullets.label: Clear criteria, communication channels,
bullets.text: Clear criteria, communication channels, transport arrangements and receiving-team coordination are essential — especially in rural or resource-limited settings.

bullets.label: Maternal death, severe morbidity, stillbirth
bullets.text: Maternal death, severe morbidity, stillbirth and neonatal deterioration should be reviewed respectfully to identify clinical and system learning.

bullets.label: Workload, fatigue, hierarchy and unclear roles
bullets.text: Workload, fatigue, hierarchy and unclear roles contribute to missed deterioration. Stronger controls redesign the system rather than relying solely on reminders.

cards.title: Section 2 — Clinical Example & Takeaways
cards.body: Clinical Example

bullets.label: A review of delayed postpartum haemorrhage
bullets.text: A review of delayed postpartum haemorrhage responses finds inconsistent emergency equipment and uncertainty about team roles.

bullets.label: Look beyond individual blame — strengthen the connection between monitoring and response to drive measurable change.
Role cards introduced for every team member
Regular drills embedded in the rota

cards.title: SECTION 3
cards.body: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation

bullets.label: Global Nursing Professionals use data and
bullets.text: Global Nursing Professionals use data and evidence to improve antenatal, intrapartum, postnatal and newborn outcomes. Improvement must be specific, practical and evaluated consistently over time.

cards.title: Section 3 — QI Framework
cards.body: Measure & Evaluate

bullets.label: Effective quality improvement begins with
bullets.text: Effective quality improvement begins with clearly defining the problem before selecting a solution. Each stage must be completed methodically — from identifying the priority through to measuring whether improvement benefits all families equitably.

cards.title: Section 3 — Priorities, Evidence & Equity
cards.body: Choosing Improvement Priorities

bullets.label: A service identifies high newborn hypothermia
bullets.text: A service identifies high newborn hypothermia rates. The team introduces immediate drying, uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact, warm transport and temperature documentation. Rates improve — and the team verifies consistent application across all birth settings.

bullets.label: Into usable pathways, not just policy documents
Does improvement benefit all families equally?

cards.title: SECTION 4
cards.body: Digital Maternity Care and Global Maternal-Newborn Health

bullets.label: Digital records, remote monitoring, telehealth
bullets.text: Digital records, remote monitoring, telehealth and decision-support tools can improve maternity care — but also introduce privacy, access and automation risks. Global Nursing Professionals use technology critically and equitably.

cards.title: Section 4 — Digital Tools and Global Equity
cards.body: Digital Maternity Records

bullets.label: Shared electronic records improve continuity,
bullets.text: Shared electronic records improve continuity, but incomplete data may create false confidence. Critical information must always be verified.

bullets.label: Telehealth extends antenatal and postnatal
bullets.text: Telehealth extends antenatal and postnatal support — provided clear escalation pathways exist for women without digital access.

bullets.label: Electronic alerts assist clinicians but do not
bullets.text: Electronic alerts assist clinicians but do not replace professional assessment. Alert fatigue and automation bias require ongoing attention.

bullets.label: Reducing maternal and neonatal mortality
bullets.text: Reducing maternal and neonatal mortality requires skilled care, timely referral, essential medicines and removal of social and geographic barriers.

bullets.label: A regional service introduces telehealth for
bullets.text: A regional service introduces telehealth for high-risk antenatal follow-up. Leaders identify that some women have limited internet access and arrange community-based monitoring and telephone support.

bullets.label: Outcome: Technology expands care without excluding vulnerable families.
Plan for privacy, downtime and digital exclusion
Adapt global evidence to local resources

cards.title: The GNPS Learning Pathway
cards.body: Programme 6 sits within a structured three-level progression designed to build expertise from foundational practice to global leadership.

bullets.label: Build strong foundations in pregnancy, labour, postnatal and newborn care
Manage high-risk maternity and neonatal care within international systems
Lead quality, safety, equity and innovation in maternal-newborn services

cards.title: Programme Complete
cards.body: By completing GNPS Programme 6 — Level 3, you have developed the advanced perspective of a Global Nursing Professional. You are prepared to:

bullets.label: To equitable maternal and newborn healthcare — locally and globally

cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 6 · Level 3 — Global Nursing Professional

bullets.label: Maternal and Newborn Nursing — Supporting Mothers and Newborns

cards.title: Section 1: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
cards.body: Leadership in maternal and newborn care means building services where women and families are treated with dignity, staff can raise concerns freely, and evidence-based care is delivered reliably.

bullets.label: Global Nursing Professionals model respectful practice and strengthen clinical governance at every level of care.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Describe the core leadership responsibilities in maternity services.
Promote respectful and psychologically safe care for women and families.
Support staff competence and preparedness for obstetric emergencies.
Strengthen governance structures and accountability within the unit.

cards.title: Respectful Maternity Care
cards.body: Respectful maternity care is both an ethical responsibility and a patient safety imperative. Every woman deserves:

bullets.label: Maintained throughout labour, birth and postnatal care.
Clear, honest communication enabling shared decision-making.
Care free from bias, mistreatment or coercion at all times.

cards.title: Psychological Safety in Maternity Teams
cards.body: Why It Matters

bullets.label: When staff feel psychologically safe, they are
bullets.text: When staff feel psychologically safe, they are more likely to question abnormal findings, request senior support, and report near misses — enabling earlier intervention and preventing harm.

bullets.label: Psychological safety is a measurable quality indicator — not just a cultural aspiration.
Raise concerns without fear of humiliation or blame.
Honest reporting drives learning and system improvement.

cards.title: Competence Through Simulation
cards.body: Regular education, team drills and simulation exercises build the confidence and clinical reflexes needed to manage obstetric emergencies effectively.

bullets.label: Rapid recognition and stepwise response to postpartum haemorrhage.
Safe seizure management, magnesium sulphate protocols and monitoring.
Coordinated manoeuvres practised under timed simulation conditions.
Airway management, ventilation and team roles rehearsed regularly.

cards.title: Clinical Governance Framework
cards.body: Robust clinical governance provides the oversight needed for consistent, safe practice across the maternity unit.

bullets.label: Data identifies gaps and tracks improvement over time.
Staff competencies are verified and maintained formally.
Structured reviews promote learning without blame.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Activating the Emergency Team
cards.body: The Challenge

bullets.label: A maternity unit observes that junior staff
bullets.text: A maternity unit observes that junior staff hesitate to activate the emergency team when concerned about a deteriorating patient — delaying critical intervention.

bullets.label: Introduced multidisciplinary simulation drills for realistic practice
Established clear escalation criteria visible to all staff
Embedded supportive debriefing after every emergency event
Outcome: Emergency activation became earlier, staff confidence measurably improved.

cards.title: The Leadership Pathway
cards.body: Build Culture

bullets.label: Create space where concerns are heard
Effective maternity leadership connects values,
bullets.text: Effective maternity leadership connects values, culture, clinical skill, and governance into a unified cycle of continuous improvement.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Measurable Standards

bullets.label: Make respectful care a formal, auditable expectation — not an aspiration.
Build a culture where every team member can speak up safely.
Use simulation to rehearse emergencies before they happen.
Link policy with leadership presence and ongoing governance review.

cards.title: Improving Maternal and Neonatal Safety Systems
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 6 · Level 3

cards.title: Why Systems Thinking Matters
cards.body: Preventable maternal and newborn harm rarely has a single cause. The most common contributing factors include:

bullets.label: Failure to identify deterioration early enough to intervene
Unclear handovers, incomplete reporting, hierarchy barriers
Inconsistent criteria and poor coordination between teams

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: What You Will Be Able to Do

bullets.label: After completing this section, you should be able to:
Apply systems thinking to maternal and neonatal safety events
Improve escalation and referral systems for timely response
Use perinatal and maternal review to support team learning
Propose practical, evidence-based risk reduction strategies

cards.title: Deterioration Systems
cards.body: Maternal early warning tools and neonatal observation pathways are only effective when completed accurately and linked to a timely, structured response.

bullets.label: Regular, complete vital sign documentation using validated tools
Clear trigger thresholds that activate a clinical response immediately
Defined team roles and treatment protocols activated without delay

cards.title: Core Concept
cards.body: Referral & Transfer Pathways

bullets.label: Effective referral is especially critical in
bullets.text: Effective referral is especially critical in rural and resource-limited settings, where distance and infrastructure amplify risk.

bullets.label: Every minute matters in obstetric emergencies — a pre-agreed pathway saves lives.

cards.title: Reviewing Serious Events
cards.body: Maternal deaths, severe morbidity, stillbirth, and neonatal deterioration must be reviewed respectfully and systematically — not to assign blame, but to generate learning.

bullets.label: Examine clinical decision-making, system delays, and contributory factors
Identify near-miss events as learning opportunities before harm recurs
Apply perinatal review frameworks with sensitivity and rigour

cards.title: Core Concept
cards.body: Human Factors in Maternity Care

bullets.label: Individual errors are rarely the root cause. Work conditions shape outcomes.
Overloaded staff miss subtle signs of deterioration
Junior staff may hesitate to escalate concerns to seniors
Poor placement of emergency supplies causes critical delays
Ambiguity during emergencies leads to inaction or duplication

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: Postpartum Haemorrhage: A System Improvement Story

bullets.label: Unclear roles and variable trolley setup
Standard trolleys, role cards, regular drills
Faster responses and more reliable treatment
This real-world example demonstrates how
bullets.text: This real-world example demonstrates how standardising equipment and clarifying roles during emergency drills can produce measurable, sustained improvements in patient outcomes.

cards.title: The Right Approach to Safety
cards.body: ❌ Blame-Focused Thinking

bullets.label: Focus on who made the error
Individual retraining as the only response
Ask why conditions allowed the error

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Look Beyond Individual Blame

bullets.label: Systems and conditions — not individuals alone — drive most adverse events
Early warning tools are only as strong as the escalation pathway behind them
Consistency in emergencies reduces cognitive load and delays
Serious-event review should produce measurable, accountable improvements

decks.title: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 6 - Level 3 - Section 3 - Global Nurse Professional - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 6 · Supporting Mothers and Newborns

cards.title: Introduction
cards.body: Global Nursing Professionals use data and evidence to improve outcomes across the full continuum of maternity care — antenatal, intrapartum, postnatal, and newborn. Improvement must be specific, practical, and evaluated over time to create lasting change at the bedside and across care systems.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Identify clinical priorities using real patient outcome data.
Use structured quality-improvement frameworks in practice.
Convert guidelines into practical maternity care workflows.
Assess patient experience and identify unequal access to care.

cards.title: Choosing Improvement Priorities
cards.body: Not all problems can be tackled at once. Effective teams begin by identifying the highest-impact issue in their clinical setting using local data.

cards.title: Testing Change: The QI Cycle
cards.body: Define the Problem

bullets.label: Structured testing prevents large-scale rollout
bullets.text: Structured testing prevents large-scale rollout of unproven changes. Each cycle generates evidence to guide the next iteration — ensuring improvements are safe, effective, and sustainable before becoming standard practice.

cards.title: Evidence Translation
cards.body: Guidelines sitting in policy documents do not change outcomes — translation into action does.

bullets.label: Convert guidelines into clear, step-by-step clinical care pathways.
Deliver targeted training so all staff understand the evidence base.
Ensure the right tools are available at the point of care.
Embed evidence into records and audit tools to sustain change.

cards.title: Measurement and Equity
cards.body: Measuring improvement requires three lenses working together. But measurement alone is not enough — data must be disaggregated across populations to reveal hidden inequities in access and outcomes.

bullets.label: Ask: Does our improvement benefit all families
bullets.text: Ask: Does our improvement benefit all families equally? If certain communities show no benefit, the pathway must be reviewed.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Newborn Hypothermia
cards.body: The Problem

bullets.label: A maternity service identifies elevated rates
bullets.text: A maternity service identifies elevated rates of newborn hypothermia through audit data, prompting a focused quality improvement response.

cards.title: The Result: Consistent, Equitable Care
cards.body: Hypothermia rates improve — and the team goes further, verifying the pathway is applied consistently across all birth settings, not just well-resourced ones.

bullets.label: Data reveals a clinical problem that warrants urgent attention.
A structured, evidence-based protocol is designed and tested.
Rates decline; outcomes improve measurably for newborns.
Equity review confirms benefits reach every family and every setting.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Define First

bullets.label: Always define the problem clearly before
bullets.text: Always define the problem clearly before selecting any solution. Evidence-free decisions risk wasted effort and patient harm.

bullets.label: Evidence must become a reliable workflow — not just a guideline stored in a folder.
Track outcomes and unintended consequences. No change is without risk.
Improvement that does not reach every community is incomplete. Equity is not optional — it is the standard.

cards.title: Digital Maternity Care & Global Maternal-Newborn Health
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 6 · Level 3 · Section 4

cards.title: Section Overview
cards.body: "Healthy beginnings. Compassionate care."

bullets.label: Digital records, remote monitoring, telehealth
bullets.text: Digital records, remote monitoring, telehealth and decision-support tools can transform maternity care — but only when used critically, equitably, and with professional judgement at the centre.

bullets.label: Evaluate technology used in maternity care
Contribute to maternal and neonatal improvement

cards.title: Digital Maternity Records
cards.body: Shared electronic health records improve continuity of care across services — but they also carry risks that every Global Nursing Professional must understand.

bullets.label: Seamless information sharing across antenatal,
bullets.text: Seamless information sharing across antenatal, intrapartum and postnatal services reduces duplication and supports safer handover.

bullets.label: Incomplete or incorrect data can create false
bullets.text: Incomplete or incorrect data can create false confidence. Always verify critical clinical information — never rely solely on the digital record.

cards.title: Remote & Rural Maternity Care
cards.body: Expanding Access Through Telehealth

bullets.label: Telehealth and remote monitoring can bridge
bullets.text: Telehealth and remote monitoring can bridge geographical barriers, extending antenatal and postnatal support to women in underserved communities.

bullets.label: Key requirements for safe remote care:
Clear escalation pathways for deteriorating patients
Alternative support for those without digital access
Telephone support as a backup channel

cards.title: Decision Support & Automation
cards.body: Electronic alerts and fetal-monitoring technologies assist clinicians — but professional judgement always takes precedence.

bullets.label: Frequent automated alerts may lead nurses to
bullets.text: Frequent automated alerts may lead nurses to dismiss genuine warnings. Maintain active clinical assessment alongside electronic monitoring.

bullets.label: Over-reliance on system recommendations can
bullets.text: Over-reliance on system recommendations can erode critical thinking. Technology supports — it does not replace — your assessment.

bullets.label: Nurses remain accountable for all clinical decisions, regardless of what decision-support tools recommend.

cards.title: Global Health & Equity
cards.body: Reducing maternal and neonatal mortality demands more than technology — it requires a systems-level commitment to equitable, respectful care.

bullets.label: Skilled birth attendants at every delivery
Dignity, cultural safety and person-centred care

cards.title: Addressing Barriers
cards.body: Social & Geographic Inequity in Maternity Care

bullets.label: Even the most advanced digital tools cannot compensate for systemic inequity. Global Nursing Professionals must:
Identify vulnerable women in their caseload
Adapt global evidence to local realities
Escalate equity concerns through appropriate channels

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: Telehealth in Practice: Balancing Access and Inclusion

bullets.label: A regional service introduces telehealth for
bullets.text: A regional service introduces telehealth for high-risk antenatal follow-up, aiming to reduce unnecessary hospital visits and support women closer to home.

bullets.label: Leaders identify that a significant proportion
bullets.text: Leaders identify that a significant proportion of women have limited or no internet access — risking digital exclusion of the most vulnerable.

bullets.label: Community-based monitoring stations and
bullets.text: Community-based monitoring stations and telephone support are arranged, ensuring technology expands care without excluding vulnerable families.

bullets.label: Always assess digital access before implementing telehealth pathways
Arrange alternatives before a gap in care occurs
Involve community partners in service design
Document alternative arrangements clearly in the care plan
Technology should widen access — never narrow it.

cards.title: Putting It Into Practice
cards.body: Apply these principles every time digital tools intersect with maternity care.

bullets.label: These four principles form the foundation of
bullets.text: These four principles form the foundation of safe, equitable and effective digital maternity practice for Global Nursing Professionals.

cards.title: Section 4 Key Takeaways
cards.body: Technology supports — it never replaces — clinical judgement

bullets.label: Always verify records and maintain active assessment alongside digital tools.
Ensure alternatives exist for patients without internet or device access before gaps arise.
Seamless maternity care requires collaboration across community, primary and secondary services.
Adapt global evidence to local needs
Equity in maternal-newborn health demands culturally responsive, resource-aware practice.
